It operates through Google Services, Google Cloud, and Other Bets segments. The Google Services segment provides products and services, including ads, Android, Chrome, devices, Gmail, Google Drive, Google Maps, Google Photos, Google Play, Search, and YouTube. It is also involved in the sale of apps and in-app purchases and digital content in Google Play and YouTube; and devices, as well as the provision of YouTube consumer subscription services, such as YouTube TV, YouTube Music and Premium, NFL Sunday Ticket, and Google One. The Google Cloud segment offers consumption-based fees and subscriptions for AI solutions, including AI infrastructure, Vertex AI platform, and Gemini enterprise. It also provides cybersecurity, and data and analytics services; Google Workspace that include cloud-based communication and collaboration tools for enterprises, such as Calendar, Gmail, Docs, Drive, and Meet; and other enterprise services. The Other Bets segment sells transportation and internet services. Ticker: $GOOGLWhat I'm doing: AvoidingCurrent price: US$338.23 Estimated value: US$146.91 Upside: -56.6% Expected IRR: 6.9%-Investment thesisAlphabet is priced as if almost everything goes right at once.At about $338 a share, the market values the business at roughly $4.1 trillion. That is not automatically wrong. Alphabet owns one of the strongest consumer and business ecosystems on the planet. Search, YouTube, Android, Maps, Chrome, and Google Cloud give it reach that few firms can match. But the current price bakes in a rare mix of outcomes: fast growth, very high profitability, and surprisingly light reinvestment needs.When I test that mix against how the business actually works, I struggle to make it add up. On my numbers, fair value is closer to $147 a share, with a wide range around that, roughly $93 on a cautious view and $214 on an optimistic one.The gap comes down to three assumptions that matter far more than the rest.The first is growth. Alphabet is already enormous. Recent revenue is about $350bn a year. When a firm is that large, “high-teens growth” is not just a forecast. It is a claim about how much new demand it can create and capture year after year, while competitors fight harder and regulators watch closer. I do expect Alphabet to grow well. Cloud adoption still has room to run. AI features can make products stickier and can open new paid use cases. But I do not assume a permanent step-change that keeps group growth near 19% for long. My base case sits nearer 12% for the earlier part of the next decade, fading towards a stable rate over time.That difference sounds small. It is not. In a long-duration equity story, a few points of growth compound into a very different terminal cash flow.The second assumption is long-run margin. The market is effectively paying as if Alphabet can sustain net income margins in the mid-40s. That is an extraordinary level for a company that is still spending heavily to defend its core franchise and build new capacity.Alphabet’s recent economics look strong, but they do not point to mid-40s net margins as a stable resting place. Net profit margins have tended to sit in a wide but familiar band: high 20s to mid 30s, with 2024 around the low 30s. To get to a stable 45%+ net margin, Alphabet would need unusually large operating leverage while holding down the costs that naturally rise with scale: traffic acquisition, content costs, and depreciation from technical infrastructure.I also think the revenue mix matters more than people admit. Search and YouTube advertising are still the profit engine. But Cloud, subscriptions, and devices are a growing share of the whole. Those lines can improve with scale, yet they rarely carry the same margin profile as mature ads. If Cloud grows faster than the group (as I expect), it can lift growth but still dilute peak margins. AI adds another pressure point. Training and serving large models is not free, and the bill shows up in chips, power, and data centres.So I assume a stable net margin nearer 29%. That is not a bearish number. It still implies a business with major scale advantages. It simply avoids assuming Alphabet becomes structurally more profitable than its own history while it ramps one of the largest infrastructure cycles in the industry.The third assumption is capital efficiency, and it is the one most investors ignore. In simple terms, I ask: how much extra investment does Alphabet need to turn growth into cash for shareholders?A useful way to think about this is “sales to equity”: how many dollars of revenue the firm generates for each dollar of equity tied up in the business. A higher ratio means the firm can grow without having to pour as much money back in. A lower ratio means growth requires more reinvestment.Alphabet is often described as capital-light, and in some ways it is. Much of its value sits in software, data, and distribution. But the AI build makes capital intensity real again. Data centres, servers, and specialised chips expand the asset base. If I treat long-lived intangibles as investments rather than period costs, the business has not looked like a pure cash machine that can grow effortlessly. Historically, the sales-to-equity ratio has sat around 0.7. The market’s implied view is closer to 1.2, which would mean Alphabet can scale revenue while barely adding to its invested base.I do not buy that. Not in a world where AI compute and Cloud capacity are strategic weapons. My base case nudges capital efficiency up only modestly to about 0.8, largely because buybacks can help, but not enough to offset the sheer weight of reinvestment required to stay ahead.Put those three pieces together and the valuation changes sharply.On my base case, I discount free cash flow to equity over a ten-year fade period, then assume a stable growth rate of about 3.5%. I use a cost of equity in the low double digits (around 11.5% initially, easing modestly in the stable period). I also subtract specific obligations that belong ahead of common shareholders, including a material legal contingency already carried as a liability. The result is an equity value a little under $1.8 trillion, which works out to roughly $147 per share on a share count a touch over 12 billion.That is a long way below $338. It is also not a “disruption is coming tomorrow” story. It is a “great business, too expensive” story.One way I sanity-check this is to flip the model around. If the current price is right, what has to be true? The answer is uncomfortable. The price implies a combination of about 18.8% revenue growth, a stable net margin around 45.5%, and capital efficiency around 1.2 sales-to-equity. Any one of those could be debated in isolation. All three together is a heroic ask.So what would change the narrative? I watch three near-term pressure points.First, the next earnings and guidance cycle matters because it forces management to put numbers on investment. If Alphabet keeps talking about elevated spend on AI infrastructure, the “easy margin expansion” story weakens. Second, any clearer disclosure on capex, buybacks, and stock-based pay will show whether capital efficiency is improving or whether investment simply absorbs the gains. Third, antitrust remedies and regulatory outcomes can shift the long-run profit pool in ways that are hard to model but impossible to ignore.I also take the upside seriously. AI could lift ad performance enough to raise pricing and conversion. Cloud could scale faster and become meaningfully more profitable as utilisation improves. Alphabet could also lean harder into buybacks and shrink the equity base. If those things happen together, my $214 bull case starts to look conservative, even if the current price still looks rich.But I come back to the same point. At $338, the market is paying today for a decade that has not happened yet. It is paying for fast growth at massive scale, structurally higher margins than history, and lighter reinvestment than the AI arms race suggests. I would rather start from what the business has proved it can do, then pay a sensible price for the improvements that are plausible.Right now, the price looks like the improvement is already guaranteed.-Resources:📊 Download the editable Excel valuation model: https://valuationbot.ai/api/blog-files/1b60709d-26e4-4da5-bbd7-4c2d41757923.xlsx📑 Download the full report: https://valuationbot.ai/api/blog-files/685ec06a-0fd8-46c5-94bb-aec42fc53136.pdf Trailing total returns as of 4/1/2026, which may include dividends or other distributions. Fair Value Dividend Score Hiring Score Insider Sentiment Score View More Alphabet Earnings: Continued Momentum on Cloud and Search as Capital Expenses Set to Mount Alphabet is a holding company that wholly owns internet giant Google. The California-based company derives slightly less than 90% of its revenue from Google services, the vast majority of which is advertising sales. Alongside online ads, Google services houses sales stemming from Google’s subscription services (YouTube TV and YouTube Music, among others), platforms (sales and in-app purchases on Play Store), and devices (Chromebooks, Pixel smartphones, and smart home products such as Chromecast). Google’s cloud computing platform accounts for roughly 10% of Alphabet’s revenue. The firm’s investments in up-and-coming technologies such as self-driving cars (Waymo), health (Verily), and internet access (Google Fiber) make up the rest. On a regular basis, we make tactical adjustments to the models, based on our outlooks for the various segments of the capital markets. Performance matters, and we monitor it closely. Looking ahead, from an asset-allocation standpoint, our Stock-Bond Barometer model still sees both asset classes near fair value, so portfolio weights ultimately will depend on strategic factors. We are market-weight on large-cap stocks at this stage of the market cycle. We favor large-caps for growth exposure and financial strength, as well as exposure to the Tech sector. Small- and mid-caps offer better valuation. Our recommended exposure to small- and mid-caps is 15% of equity allocation, in line with the benchmark weighting. One of the market surprises in 2025 was the performance of global stocks, which turned in impressive results. We expect the long-term trend favoring U.S. stocks to re-emerge ultimately, given volatile global economic, political, geopolitical, and currency conditions. That said, international stocks still offer favorable near-term valuations, and we target 20% of equity exposure to the group. In terms of growth and value, over the longer term, we anticipate that growth, led by the Tech sector, will top returns from value, led by Energy, Real Estate, and Materials, due to favorable secular and demographic trends.
